overview.title: Interpreting the pretrained LSTM result; chapter summary begins
overview.subsection: 14.5.5 Using the pretrained embedding for classification
overview.main_topic: Why the pretrained LSTM only matches the set-based models (it is still data-constrained), why Transformers trained on lots of ordered text will do better, the cost-effectiveness of set models, and the first half of the chapter summary (tokenization, its three steps and three types, set vs. sequence models)
overview.central_idea: Sequence models are expressive enough to beat bag-of-words models but need far more ordered training data than 20,000 reviews; until that data (or pretraining on large text corpora) is available, cheap set-based models like the bigram model are hard to beat per unit of compute.
overview.importance: It closes the chapter's experimental arc and motivates chapter 15: the answer to data-hungry sequence models is large-scale pretraining of Transformers, not giving up on word order. It also gives a practical rule for constrained settings.
learning_objectives: Place the pretrained LSTM's 89.1% between the unigram (88.4%) and bigram (90.1%) models
Explain what 'data-constrained' means for the LSTM
Explain why Transformers pretrained on large text corpora overcome this
Argue when a set-based model is the most cost-effective choice
Recall the three tokenization steps and three tokenization types
Contrast set models and sequence models
prerequisites: Results of p.426, p.428, p.437 and p.442

summary:
The page first interprets the result of p.442. With pretrained embedding weights, the LSTM's test accuracy (0.89139) is **roughly the same as the set-based models**: slightly better than the unigram bag-of-words model (0.88388, p.426) and slightly worse than the bigram model (0.90116, p.428).

Is learning on the full ordered sequence a bad idea, then? No. The authors argue the LSTM is ***still data-constrained***: it is expressive enough that with enough movie reviews it would easily outperform set-based approaches, but it needs much more training on ***ordered data*** before reaching its performance ceiling. That problem is solvable with enough compute. The next chapter introduces the **Transformer**, which is slightly better at learning dependencies across long token sequences, but, more importantly, is typically trained on large amounts of English text *including word order*, so it learns roughly a statistical form of the grammatical patterns of language. Those word-order patterns are exactly what the small LSTM lacks the data to learn.

Still, simple set-based regression approaches like the bigram model give a lot of **"bang for your buck"**: they are lightning-fast and tiny compared to billion-parameter LLMs. When compute is limited and some accuracy can be sacrificed, set models are often the most cost-effective approach.

The **chapter summary** begins:

- Every text modeling problem starts with **tokenization**: turning text into integers.
- Tokenization has three steps: **standardization** (normalize), **splitting** (into tokens), **indexing** (assign integer IDs).
- Three main types: **character**, **word**, and **subword**; with an expressive model and enough data, subword is usually best.
- NLP models differ mainly in how they treat token order: **set models** (presence/absence of tokens, or of bigrams/trigrams; very fast) versus **sequence models** (ordered tokens; need lots of data).

The summary continues on p.444 with embeddings and pretraining.

paragraphs.excerpt: With the pretrained embedding weights, we have boosted our LSTM performance to roughly
paragraphs.what_it_says: Pretraining lifted the LSTM to roughly the level of the set-based models: slightly better than unigram, slightly worse than bigram.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Numerically: unigram 0.88388 < pretrained LSTM 0.89139 < bigram 0.90116. The gain from pretraining (+~5 points over 0.84436) is real, but the much larger and slower model still does not beat a 30,001-parameter logistic regression on bigram features.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It forces the honest question that the next paragraph answers: is word order useless, or is something else holding the sequence model back?

terminology.meaning: The bag-of-words model: one weight per single word (p.427 notes the equivalence).

paragraphs.excerpt: This may seem like a bit of a letdown after all the work we put in.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The disappointment is explained: the LSTM is still data-constrained and would win with many more movie reviews. Enough compute solves this; Transformers (next chapter) are slightly better at long-range dependencies but mainly benefit from being trained on large amounts of ordered English text, learning statistical grammatical patterns. Meanwhile set-based models like the bigram model offer great value: lightning-fast, few parameters compared with billion-parameter LLMs, and often the most cost-effective choice when compute is limited and some accuracy can be sacrificed.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Two separate claims are made. (1) **Capacity vs. data**: a sequence model can represent order-dependent patterns (negation, "not bad", long-range qualifiers), but learning them requires many examples of ordered text. CBOW pretraining only taught *which words co-occur*, as an unordered bag, so the LSTM still had to learn order from 20,000 labeled reviews. Transformers pretrained as language models learn order from billions of tokens, which is why the authors expect them to do better. (2) **Cost-effectiveness**: the bigram model is about 90% accurate with tens of thousands of parameters and seconds of CPU training.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It frames chapter 15: the fix is pretraining on ordered text at scale, not a cleverer recurrent cell. It also teaches an engineering judgment: always benchmark a cheap baseline before reaching for a large model.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Note (beyond the book): CBOW's averaging (GlobalAveragePooling1D, p.440) discards order inside the context window, so the pretrained embedding contains no word-order information at all. The authors' 'ordered data' emphasis is consistent with this: what's missing is pretraining that uses order, which language modeling (p.445 onward) provides. The book later reports a fine-tuned pretrained Transformer reaching 93% on this task (chapter 15).

terminology.meaning: Performance is limited by the amount of training data rather than by model capacity or compute per step.
The best accuracy an architecture could reach given unlimited data and training.
Logistic regression on multi-hot token (or n-gram) presence features.

paragraphs.excerpt: All text modeling problems involve a preprocessing step where text is broken up
paragraphs.what_it_says: Every text modeling problem includes tokenization: breaking text up and turning it into integers.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Neural networks operate on numeric tensors, so text must be converted to integer IDs before an Embedding, multi-hot encoding or any other layer can use it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Tokenization choices (vocabulary size, splitting rule) shape every model downstream, including what max_tokens means.

terminology.meaning: Converting raw text to a sequence of integer token IDs.

paragraphs.excerpt: Tokenization can be divided into three steps: standardization, splitting, and indexing.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Standardization normalizes text, splitting breaks it into tokens, indexing assigns each token a unique integer ID.
paragraphs.what_it_means: E.g. 'The Cat!' -> standardize -> 'the cat' -> split -> ['the', 'cat'] -> index -> [2, 57]. In Keras the TextVectorization layer bundles all three.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Seeing the steps separately lets you customize each (e.g. keeping punctuation, splitting into subwords).

terminology.meaning: Normalizing text, e.g. lowercasing and removing punctuation.
Breaking text into units (characters, words, subwords).
Mapping each token to a unique integer through a vocabulary.

paragraphs.excerpt: There are three main types of tokenization: character, word, and subword tokenization.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Character, word and subword tokenization are the three main types; with an expressive enough model and enough data, subword tokenization is usually the most effective.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Characters give tiny vocabularies but very long sequences; words give short sequences but huge vocabularies and many unknown tokens; subwords (e.g. BPE) balance the two.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Subword tokenization is what the Transformers and LLMs of chapters 15-16 use.

terminology.meaning: Splitting words into frequent pieces so rare words are built from known parts.

paragraphs.excerpt: NLP models differ primarily in handling the order of input tokens:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Set models discard most order information and learn simple, fast models from token presence or absence; bigram or trigram models consider two or three consecutive tokens; set models are very fast to train and deploy. Sequence models learn from the ordered token sequence and need large amounts of data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the chapter's central dichotomy in one bullet, and the results above illustrate it: the bigram set model was the best performer on 20,000 reviews, while the sequence model is limited by data.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Choosing between the two families is a trade-off between cost, data availability, and the accuracy ceiling.

terminology.meaning: A model that sees the input as an unordered set (or bag) of tokens or n-grams.
A model that processes tokens in order (RNN, 1D convnet, Transformer).

concepts.name: Data-constrained model
concepts.definition: A model whose accuracy is limited by the amount of training data rather than by its capacity.
concepts.intuition: A powerful learner with too few examples memorizes instead of generalizing.
concepts.technical: Symptoms: high train accuracy with a large train-validation gap (the LSTM hit 99% train accuracy, p.437) and gains from extra (even unlabeled) data via pretraining.
concepts.significance: Explains why the LSTM does not beat set models here, and why pretraining at scale is the way forward.
concepts.misconception: A data-constrained model is not a bad model; with more data it can surpass simpler ones.

concepts.name: Set-based (bag-of-words / n-gram) models
concepts.definition: Models that use only the presence or absence of tokens or n-grams.
concepts.intuition: Count which words (or word pairs) appear; ignore where.
concepts.technical: Logistic regression on multi-hot vectors: 20,001 parameters for unigrams, 30,001 for bigrams in this chapter.
concepts.significance: Cheap, fast and strong baselines: "bang for your buck".
concepts.misconception: They are not useless just because they ignore order; local order can be injected with n-grams.

concepts.name: Sequence models
concepts.definition: Models that ingest the ordered token sequence.
concepts.intuition: Can tell "not bad" from "bad, not"... but must learn such patterns from data.
concepts.significance: Higher performance ceiling; require large data or pretraining.
concepts.misconception: Ordered input does not automatically mean better accuracy on small datasets.

concepts.name: Tokenization
concepts.definition: Standardization, splitting and indexing of text into integer IDs.
concepts.intuition: Turning text into a list of dictionary page numbers.
concepts.technical: Character, word, or subword units; Keras TextVectorization implements the pipeline.
concepts.significance: The first step of every text model.
concepts.misconception: Tokenization is not just splitting on spaces; standardization and indexing matter too.

deeper.title: Why CBOW pretraining was not enough
deeper.body: Beyond the book's wording: CBOW averages the eight context embeddings, so it learns which words co-occur but nothing about order. The LSTM thus starts with good *word* representations but must still learn *order-dependent* patterns (negation scope, contrast like "good acting, but terrible plot") from 20,000 labeled reviews. Language-model pretraining of Transformers (chapter 15) predicts tokens from ordered context, so order patterns are learned from unlabeled text too, which matches the authors' emphasis on "ordered data".

deeper.title: A cost-benefit view of the chapter's models
deeper.body:
| Model | Params (approx.) | Test acc. |
|---|---|---|
| Unigram bag-of-words (p.426) | 20,001 | 0.884 |
| Bigram (p.428) | 30,001 | 0.901 |
| One-hot LSTM (p.432) | ~15 M | 0.848 |
| Embedding LSTM (p.437) | ~2 M | 0.844 |
| Pretrained-embedding LSTM (p.442) | ~2 M | 0.891 |

The bigram model is roughly 65x smaller than the best LSTM and more accurate. Parameter counts for the LSTMs are the book's rounded figures.

deeper.title: Analogy: a translator with a phrasebook
deeper.body: A set model is like a tourist with a phrasebook who spots key words ("great", "awful") and guesses the mood: quick and usually right. A sequence model is like someone learning the grammar: eventually far better, but only after hearing a great deal of the language.

visualizations.title: IMDb test accuracy of the chapter's models
visualizations.why: The first paragraph compares the pretrained LSTM with the unigram and bigram models; this chart puts all of the chapter's reported test accuracies side by side.

misconceptions.claim: The result shows word order does not help sentiment classification.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say the LSTM is data-constrained; with much more ordered data it would easily outperform set models.

misconceptions.claim: Transformers win mainly because their architecture handles long sequences.
misconceptions.correction: The book says they are only slightly better at long dependencies; the critical factor is training on large amounts of ordered text.

misconceptions.claim: You should always use the largest model available.
misconceptions.correction: With limited compute, set models are often the most cost-effective choice.

takeaways: The pretrained LSTM (0.891) lands between unigram (0.884) and bigram (0.901).
The LSTM is still data-constrained: it needs much more ordered data to reach its ceiling.
Transformers help mainly because they are trained on large amounts of ordered text.
Set models give the best accuracy per unit of compute; use them when resources are tight.
Tokenization = standardization + splitting + indexing; subword is usually best with enough data and capacity.
Set models ignore order (except n-grams); sequence models use it but are data hungry.

questions.question: According to the authors, why does the pretrained LSTM not beat the bigram model?
options: The CBOW embedding was the wrong size
questions.explanation: The book says the model is expressive enough but needs much more training on ordered data. LSTMs do model order; the embedding matched in size; nothing blames bidirectionality.

questions.question: Order the unigram, bigram and pretrained LSTM models by test accuracy.
questions.explanation: From p.426, p.442, p.428; the page says slightly better than unigram, slightly worse than bigram.

questions.question: What does the book say is the 'most critical' advantage of the Transformer models of the next chapter?
questions.answer: They are often trained on large amounts of English text including all word-order information, letting them learn statistical grammatical patterns.
questions.explanation: Being slightly better at long dependencies is secondary in the authors' account.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three tokenization steps listed in the summary?
questions.explanation: The steps are standardization, splitting and indexing. Embedding comes after tokenization, mapping IDs to vectors.

questions.question: When would you deploy a bigram set model over a sequence model?
questions.answer: When compute is limited and you can sacrifice some accuracy; set models are fast and small.
questions.explanation: The authors call them often the most cost-effective approach in that setting.

questions.question: Which tokenization type is usually most effective with an expressive model and enough data?
questions.explanation: Stated in the third summary bullet; it balances vocabulary size and sequence length.

questions.question: Can you explain why CBOW pretraining improved the LSTM but did not give it knowledge of word order?
questions.answer: CBOW averages context embeddings, so it learns co-occurrence, not order; order must still be learned from labeled data.
questions.explanation: This is an inference consistent with the book's emphasis on 'ordered data'; see p.440 for the averaging.
